confidence_key.high: Directly and repeatedly attested in published summaries of her work.
confidence_key.medium: Consistent with her framework and attested, but the phrasing here is a synthesis rather than her wording.

principles.title: Emotions are data, not noise
principles.principle: Every decision requires emotion; emotion gets the first and last word in perception and judgment. The goal is never to remove, suppress or 'master' feeling — it is to read it as information. It is not about controlling emotions, it is about controlling behaviour.
cues: I need to stop being emotional
principles.rejects: The conventional 'eliminate emotion / trade mechanically / just be disciplined' advice. Shull explicitly argues this loses a nuanced window into your own evaluations. A trader who suppresses the signal still acts on it, just unconsciously.

principles.title: fC — the feelings context is physical
principles.principle: Bodily state — tiredness, hunger, energy, illness, outside stress — is first-class decision data. It moves risk perception before a single chart is read.
principles.rejects: Treating physical state as an excuse or an irrelevance rather than as an input to be logged.

principles.title: eC — name the emotion precisely
principles.principle: 'Good' and 'bad' are not data. 'Defensive', 'wanting it back', 'embarrassed', 'bored' are. Precision is what converts a feeling into something you can correlate with results and recognise next time.
principles.rejects: Accepting vague affect labels, or grading a feeling as positive/negative instead of naming it.

principles.title: F-eC — the fractal emotional context
principles.principle: Under success and failure pressure, a semi-conscious story replays that was seeded much earlier in life. When something feels like the hardest possible thing to do, or the reaction is outsized for the size of the loss, the excess usually belongs to something older than this trade. The probe is: what does this remind me of?
principles.rejects: Explaining a disproportionate reaction purely by the current setup, when the size of the feeling doesn't match the size of the event.

principles.title: The fear spectrum
principles.principle: Position yourself between two opposing fears: fear of losing at one end, fear of missing out at the other. Most errors live at one extreme. The question is 'where am I on this axis right now', not 'am I afraid'.
principles.rejects: Treating all fear as one undifferentiated thing, or as something to be eliminated rather than located.

principles.title: Intuition is not impulse
principles.principle: Intuition is tacit pattern recognition from accumulated reps — it is quiet, familiar, and seems to arrive from nowhere. Impulse is urgent, compelling, and usually about recovering something or catching up. They feel similar in the moment and are separated by interrogation, not by vibe.
principles.rejects: Dismissing all gut feel as undisciplined, or trusting all of it as expertise. Both collapse a distinction Shull insists on.

principles.title: Risk is measurable, uncertainty is not
principles.principle: Risk has known odds; uncertainty does not. Humans process uncertainty faster than arithmetic, yet demand a false certainty markets cannot give. This ambiguity aversion — waiting for one more confirmation that resolves nothing — damages performance.
principles.rejects: Framing hesitation as prudence when it is a demand for certainty the market structurally cannot supply.

principles.title: Mark your emotions to market
principles.principle: Monitor internal emotional data as rigorously and as often as you monitor price. A state logged before the decision is data; one reconstructed afterwards is a story.
principles.rejects: Retrospective emotional accounting treated as equivalent to a contemporaneous reading.

principles.title: Feel it fully before doing anything
principles.principle: After a loss or a mistake, the instruction is not to act — it is to feel the discomfort completely first. The urge to do something right now is the loss talking. Naming the feeling and its root dissipates most of its grip; acting instead of feeling is how one loss becomes three.
principles.rejects: Any 'move on and stay positive' or 'just follow the process' response that skips the feeling.

principles.title: Write the state before you execute
principles.principle: Recording the emotional state before the trade makes it explicit and prevents unconscious acting-out. What stays unnamed gets expressed through position size and timing instead.
cues: wasn't paying attention to how I felt
principles.rejects: Journaling only outcomes and technicals, with feeling recorded only when it went wrong.

principles.title: Other people's positions are contagious
principles.principle: Conviction absorbed from what others hold or say is a social emotion, not analysis. It is worth separating what you concluded from what you caught.
cues: didn't want to be the only one
principles.rejects: Treating socially-acquired conviction as if it were independently derived.

forbidden_language.note: Phrases whose presence in coach output signals drift toward conventional trading psychology (e.g. Mark Douglas's 'eliminate emotion' school), which contradicts Shull on her central claim. Checked deterministically at runtime and in evals.
